variants.name: Boost.JSON value_from/value_to (tag_invoke)
variants.implementation_notes: In C++ the translator is a pair of customization points next to the type rather than a component: tag_invoke(value_from_tag, value&, T const&) and tag_invoke(value_to_tag<T>, value const&, T&) are found by argument-dependent lookup, and value_from/value_to dispatch to them, so the mapping is a library-defined operation (Boost.JSON, C++11). The Adapter/Translator class hierarchy is replaced by those free functions; keep an explicit translator object only when the mapping needs runtime state (loaded code lists, injected converters) or when one component has to serve several format pairs. Boost.JSON is the default here because it ships with Boost and its conversion points are the documented extension mechanism.
pitfalls: at() and to_number() throw on a malformed message: catch at the boundary and route to the invalid-message path, or a single bad payload unwinds the whole consumer.
A customization point declared in the wrong namespace is not found by ADL and the generic conversion silently takes over, so fields disappear without a compile error.
string_view/pointers returned by as_string() dangle once the temporary boost::json::value is destroyed - copy into owning storage when the translation outlives the parse.

variants.name: nlohmann/json to_json/from_json free functions
variants.implementation_notes: The same idea with the most widely used header-only library: define to_json(json&, T const&) and from_json(json const&, T&) in the namespace of T, and nlohmann's implicit conversions pick them up, with j.at() giving bounds-checked access and JSON_DISABLE_ENUM_SERIALIZATION controlling enum representation. Choose it when a header-only dependency and the library's wide ecosystem matter more than Boost integration.
pitfalls: Implicit conversions make every json assignment a translation; a missing at() turns the mapping into a silent default-construction.
Non-default-constructible members require an explicit friend declaration access hook or the library's get_to path fails to compile with confusing errors.

variants.name: protoc-generated messages (schema-first translation)
variants.implementation_notes: When the wire contract is already owned by an IDL, protoc generates the message class, its accessors and the binary parsers, so the translator degenerates into assigning the canonical model's fields from a generated message and vice versa; compatibility rules of the schema replace hand-written mapping (protobuf.dev). Use it when both sides can adopt the schema or when a schema registry already governs the exchange - the generated class covers the whole translation for that format.
pitfalls: Generated setters and ParseFrom accept partially populated messages, and unknown fields are preserved but never validated, so required-field or semantic checks must be added explicitly.
The generated code must be rebuilt in lockstep with the .proto; a stale generated class compiles against the old field numbers and corrupts the wire form.
